extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of advertising history, consumer-protection researchers, and general readers interested in historical examples of advertising fraud
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and analyze features, red flags, and modus operandi of fraudulent or deceptive advertisements and home-employment schemes as illustrated by 19th-century historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive or fabricated testimonials
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimonials with an implausible number of signatures or obvious invention; writers sometimes resort to initials when signatures would be too many to manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes the 'number of signatures he must have invented' and that 'Occasionally he breaks down... and has to fall back on initials.' Large volumes of uniformly laudatory testimonials or initials instead of full names are a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promises of easy wealth and lucrative employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements that promise easy money, rapid rise to opulence, or lucrative employment from little effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a guide to the employment of a whole life, and an easy path to opulence' and claims like 'How to make Two pounds per Week by the outlay of Ten Shillings.' Grandiose income promises unattached to concrete methods should be treated as suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for stamps or stamped addressed envelopes
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking correspondents to enclose stamps or a stamped addressed envelope as the means to receive particulars or prospectuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter describes 'off go the stamps' and many adverts asking for thirty stamps or for an 'addressed stamped envelope' to obtain a prospectus—a common tactic to extract small sums from many victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial low fee followed by demands for further fees (registration/deposit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Require an up-front small payment, then later demand larger 'registration', 'deposit' or 'security' sums to obtain the promised goods or employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: requests for five shillings for registration and five pounds deposit; one-guinea 'registration fee, materials, and instruction.' This staged-fee pattern is a hallmark of many scams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blaming postal delay or claiming packet 'lost/stolen' as an excuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulars that claim packets were delayed, lost, or stolen in transit and thus justify not delivering promised materials on time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text reproduces a circular: 'An error prevails regarding the punctual and prompt conveyance of Packets by the Post Office... you may fully expect it by the second if not by the first mail.' Such explanations are often used to stall and extract further payments or to avoid accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sending inadequate or useless 'samples' to feign fulfillment
rubrics_metrics.description: When pushed, fraudsters send trivial, irrelevant, or unusable sample items to appease victims temporarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'scraps of brown paper' said to be patterns for pen-wipers, or a parcel with odd lasts, a small boot, bits of leather, an awl and wax. Such token shipments are used to buy time while operators change names/addresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vague, anonymous, or initial-only addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of initials, cryptic addresses, or generic post-office designations (e.g., 'X. Y. Z', 'B. C. Post-office, Chichester') rather than full, verifiable contact details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text shows many letters directed to initials and multiple offices; such vagueness allows mass replies and shields the advertiser from responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand prospectuses and exclusivity claims to feign legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Pretentious titles, elaborate prospectuses, and claims of exclusivity (e.g., 'the same sermon will not be sent to any two clergymen within twenty miles') intended to create an aura of authority and scarcity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Private Office for the Supply of Sermons' and similar documents use high-sounding language and exclusivity to convince clients; these are persuasive devices and may mask fraudulent intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requiring a 'guarantee' deposit to prevent copying or for security
rubrics_metrics.description: Demanding a monetary guarantee (e.g., 10s) from prospective copyists or workers as a condition before sending materials, purportedly to prevent unauthorized copying or as security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'a guarantee of 10s. will be required from each copyist before MSS. are sent'—this 'guarantee' is often a pretext for extracting funds rather than genuine protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implausible pay rates or profit calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed calculations or asserted hourly/weekly rates that, on inspection, are unrealistic or based on optimistic assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include promises of 'never to earn less than eightpence or a shilling per hour' or the baked-potato scheme showing a 'Nett profit per week, £2 0s 0d.' Such arithmetic may be deliberately misleading or ignore real costs and market limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers/publishers possibly complicit through advertising tariffs
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that proprietors may charge extra prices for fraudulent advertisements, making them accessories to the swindle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that if 'larger prices are charged to men because their advertisements are fraudulent... the proprietors of the papers are accessories.' Awareness that some publications profited from such insertions is part of assessing risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting vulnerable or specific demographic groups with sentimental appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements crafted to appeal to particular vulnerable groups (e.g., decently-educated young women in need of employment) using sympathetic or urgent language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: adverts for 'HOME EMPLOYMENT' aimed at ladies and 'young girls' exploiting their pressing need for income. Recognize solicitations that play on desperation or social constraints as higher-risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulars that disparage institutions to deflect criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulars or notices that denigrate postal services or other institutions to explain failures or justify shortcomings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes 'This circular speaks of the post-office, and other institutions, in the most disparaging manner'—such blame-shifting is a manipulative tactic to deflect suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructions that cause customers to omit needed details (convenient 'mistakes')
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational instructions or forms that result in correspondents omitting critical information (e.g., enclosing name but omitting address) and then blaming the correspondent for non-delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: correspondents 'send only their name and address on a stamped envelope, and when ordering the Packet enclose their name and omit the address'—the advertiser then claims inability to forward the packet, creating an excuse to avoid responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home-employment schemes that force victims to buy materials and never pay for finished work
rubrics_metrics.description: Schemes that supply minimal materials, require the worker to purchase additional items, take the completed work, and then fail to remunerate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case of Mrs Dellair: victims received some materials (e.g., ten toilet-mats), had to buy extra materials themselves to finish, sent the work and received no payment—an archetypal pattern of exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent changing of names, addresses, and use of aliases
rubrics_metrics.description: Operatives routinely change names and addresses to avoid detection, prosecution, and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative describes 'a little delay enables these wandering tribes to change both names and addresses' and mentions many aliases for the same offender; lack of stable, verifiable identity is a major warning sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed circulars with blanks for reuse across trades
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass-produced circulars printed with blanks for the trade description and product name so the same form can be reused for different deceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a circular 'printed, with blanks left for description of the patterns and the name of the work'—this indicates a template-based scam designed for broad reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance-subscription or advance-payment business models used as cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Require advance subscriptions or payments (e.g., for regular sermons or parcels) payable in advance ostensibly to secure service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sermons subscription: 'subscription for three sermons weekly is four guineas per annum, payable in advance.' Advance payments with limited or unverifiable delivery history are higher risk.
